    Meta-regression with study level moderators

    Source: R/meta-regression.R
    meta_regress.Rd

    meta_regress() fits a mixed-effects meta-regression in which study level covariates (moderators) explain part of the between-study heterogeneity. The residual heterogeneity \(\tau^2\) is estimated with any of the estimators available in meta_pool(). The omnibus test of moderators (QM) is a Wald chi-squared test, or an F test when test = "hksj". The pseudo \(R^2\) compares \(\tau^2\) from the model with that of an intercept only model fitted with the same estimator.

    Usage

    meta_regress(
  .data,
  mods,
  yi = .yi,
  vi = .vi,
  method = "REML",
  test = "z",
  level = 0.95,
  study = NULL
)

    Arguments

    .data

    A <meta_es> from meta_effect_size() or any data frame with effect sizes and sampling variances.

    mods

    A one-sided formula of moderators, for example ~ ablat or ~ factor(alloc) + year. Use ~ 0 + group to drop the intercept.

    yi, vi

    <data-masking> Columns holding the effect sizes and sampling variances. Default to .yi and .vi.

    method

    Estimator of the between-study variance: "REML", "ML", "DL", "PM", "SJ" or "FE" (common effect).

    test

    "z" for normal based inference or "hksj" for the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment.

    level

    Confidence level for intervals.

    study

    <data-masking> Optional study labels. Taken from the <meta_es> when available.

    Value

    A <meta_fit> with one row per coefficient.

    References

    Thompson, S. G. and Higgins, J. P. T. (2002). How should meta-regression analyses be undertaken and interpreted? Statistics in Medicine, 21(11), 1559-1573. doi:10.1002/sim.1187

    Raudenbush, S. W. (2009). Analyzing effect sizes: random-effects models. In H. Cooper, L. V. Hedges and J. C. Valentine (Eds.), The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis (2nd ed., pp. 295-315). Russell Sage Foundation.

    Examples

    bcg <- meta_effect_size(bcg_trials, "RR",
  event1 = tpos, n1 = tpos + tneg, event2 = cpos, n2 = cpos + cneg
)
fit <- meta_regress(bcg, ~ ablat)
fit
#> # Meta-regression <meta_fit>
#> # Model: random effects, restricted maximum likelihood
#> # Measure: log risk ratio; k = 13
#> # tau^2 = 0.0763; I^2 = 68.39%; H^2 = 3.16
#> # Q(11) = 30.73, p = 0.0012
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)   0.251    0.249        1.01 0.313      -0.237     0.740 
#> 2 ablat        -0.0291   0.00720     -4.04 0.0000524  -0.0432   -0.0150
glance(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 21
#>   model_type  nobs method test    tau2 tau2.low tau2.high   tau    I2    H2
#>   <chr>      <int> <chr>  <chr>  <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 regression    13 REML   z     0.0763   0.0167     0.785 0.276  68.4  3.16
#> # ℹ 11 more variables: R2 <dbl>, QE <dbl>, df.residual <int>, p.QE <dbl>,
#> #   QM <dbl>, p.QM <dbl>, pred.low <dbl>, pred.high <dbl>, logLik <dbl>,
#> #   AIC <dbl>, BIC <dbl>
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(ablat = c(10, 30, 50)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>     .pred   .se .pred_lower .pred_upper
#>     <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 -0.0395 0.187      -0.405       0.326
#> 2 -0.622  0.107      -0.831      -0.412
#> 3 -1.20   0.172      -1.54       -0.867
